steps.b: The moon was a silver coin dropped in a dark pond.
steps.reveal: The second one compares the moon to something you already know, so a picture pops into your head. Comparisons help readers see the new through the familiar.

cards.title: Simile
cards.body: A simile compares two different things using “like” or “as”: “The bus rattled like a box of spoons.” “She was as quiet as a held breath.” The comparison shows the reader a quality: the noise, the stillness.

cards.title: Metaphor
cards.body: A metaphor says one thing IS another, with no “like” or “as”: “The classroom was a zoo.” It isn't literally true, which is what makes it bold. Metaphors feel stronger than similes because they don't hedge.

cards.title: Same idea, two ways
cards.telling: Her voice was like a warm blanket.
cards.showing: Her voice was a warm blanket.
cards.note: Both work. The metaphor is more direct; the simile is gentler.

cards.title: Spot the comparisons
cards.prompt: Tap the two things the classroom and the teacher are compared to.
cards.text: The classroom was as noisy as a zoo, and Mr Diaz was a lion tamer with a whiteboard pen.

prompts: Which comparison are you proudest of? What does it make the reader see?
Did you choose a simile or a metaphor for your strongest idea, and why?
